title: open-loop throttle notebook
content:
Purpose:
- quick scratchpad to capture open-loop (no client backpressure) experiments and odd latency/queue resonance seen last week.
- follow-ups for scheduling fixes and heuristic rejects.

Context / why this matters:
- real customers sometimes send bursts without respecting rate limits (mobile reconnects, retries). open-loop load can push internal queues to oscillate and cause p99 spikes even when average qps is modest. want reproducible micro-bench that isolates scheduler + kv-cache warmup interactions.

Hypothesis:
- the scheduler’s admission policy + batching window interacts badly with token-prefetch and kv-cache cold misses. when too many concurrent inflight requests exceed the batching cap, expensive warm-cache tokens are serialized and cause queue resonance.

Environment:
- cluster: dev-dedicated-A (4x A100-80GB, vgpu disabled)
- runtime build: serving-runtime@main (commit 6a3f2b) + small patch enabling debug metrics (PR #842)
- model: rw-instruct-13b-quant (int8) pinned v2.1
- client: synthetic open-loop generator (python, asyncio) run from loadgen-n1

Common knobs in experiments:
- arrival pattern: open-loop poisson, heavy-tailed bursts, and manual 1s microbursts
- offered QPS: 100 -> 2000 (steady), plus burst tests up to 5k for short windows
- concurrency: 8/16/32/64 simulated connections
- batching: dynamic (max_batch_size=64), fixed small (8), and disabled (no batching)
- KV cache priming: cold / partially primed / warm

Runs (selected):
- Run A (2025-02-19): poisson, offered 600 qps, concurrency 32, batching dynamic,max=64, cold cache
  - p50: 38 ms, p95: 180 ms, p99: 410 ms, throughput observed: 580 qps
  - notes: tail spikes correlate with periodic KV cache misses (trace id 0x1f2). scheduler queue length hitting 48 for ~120ms windows.

- Run B (2025-02-20): same as A but pre-warmed cache -> p50: 36ms, p95: 110ms, p99: 160ms
  - throughput stable 600 qps. conclusion: large portion of tail is cold-cache related but not all.

- Run C (2025-02-22): microbursts: base 200 qps, inject 2 bursts of 2.5k qps for 400ms, concurrency 64
  - observed: immediate p99 > 1.5s, service drops (429) after 3s, then recovery hysteresis ~12s where p95 stayed elevated
  - capture: stack traces show many requests queued at scheduler admission loop waiting for batch assembly. batching window increased under load from 12ms -> 48ms which propagated latency.

- Run D (2025-02-24): fixed small batches (max=8) with fast-reject at queue>128, open-loop 800 qps
  - p50: 44ms, p95: 150ms, p99: 260ms, throughput 780 qps
  - notes: slightly higher p50 but tail reduced. fast-reject prevented deep queueing.

Quick ASCII time-series snapshot (Run A, sample):
- t=0s: qps ramp 100->600 in 15s
- qlen: 0, 4, 9, 18, 24, 38, 48, 42, 35, 20, 8
- p99(ms): 40, 60, 90, 150, 220, 320, 410, 380, 260, 170, 120

Preliminary root-cause candidates:
1) open-loop arrival allows inflight to exceed batching capacity and causes long batching windows (batch assembly waits)
2) KV-cache cold misses create heavy execution paths that block GPU queue and increase head-of-line blocking inside runtime
3) scheduler uses global queue length metric; it needs better fairness between “short” and “long” requests (predicted by token-length and cache status)

Mitigations tried and short notes:
- fast-reject (threshold 128): reduces tail but lowers availability; good safety valve for multi-tenant clusters.
- fixed smaller max_batch_size: reduces p99 but increases cost (lower batch efficiency).
- pre-warm cache and aggressive prefix caching: best overall but requires workload cooperation / cache budget.
- per-request latency budget header to allow early prioritization: promising in two-shot sim but needs client adoption.

Open questions / TODOs:
- quantify cost delta for fixed smaller batches vs p99 reduction (rough estimate: 8->64 batch size change increases GPU token cost by ~12-15% at same throughput) -> run cost sweep next week (RW-ops-cost-sweep)
- can we implement batch-formation time cap that is adaptive (cap proportional to inflight queue and median latency)? design doc: link to JIRA-RW-1302
- instrument per-request predicted-exec-time metric from scheduler (use cheap token-count + cache-hit-prob) and route long requests to lower-priority lane -> prototype required.
- replicate on dedicated small-edition cluster (nvlink enabled) to see if GPU queueing behaviour differs.

Notes-to-self (rough):
- add histogram of per-batch assembly times in runtime debug output (already added local flag runtime.trace_batch_assembly=true)
- stash raw traces from loadgen runs in gcs://redwood-bench/open-loop/2025-02-19/ -> useful for visualizing correlation of batch_size vs p99
- follow up with Maya: can we get a customer trace that resembles open-loop arrival? she mentioned mobile-payments partner with reconnect storms.

Action items (short):
- [ ] reproduce cost vs tail tradeoff (Fern) - target by 2025-03-07
- [ ] prototype adaptive batch cap (Ethan) - spike by 2025-03-14
- [ ] add per-request predicted-exec-time metric and QA in dev cluster (Maya + Fern) - 2025-03-21

Random half-formed thought:
- trick: if client can send a small early 'intent' token (cheap preflight) that pre-populates kv keys for long responses, we can avoid heavy cold misses inside the batch. could be offered as SDK helper.

References and links:
- slack thread: #runtime-surge (see thread ts 1678452000)
- confluence sketch: https://confluence.redwood/inference/open-loop-sched-sketch
- PR where I toggled batch debug: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842

End of notebook (for now).
